他.title: 他 (he) vs 她 (she)
他.summary: 他 and 她 sound exactly the same: tā. Only the writing tells them apart, so learn to spot the left-hand side.

sections.heading: Spot the difference
sections.intro: Both are a left part plus the same right part, 也. Only the left part changes.

items.note: Left part 亻 = the “person” radical, a squashed 人.
Left part 女 = “woman”, the character you already know.

sections.heading: Tips for telling them apart
items: Look left first. A thin, upright 亻 means a person (he). A curvy 女 means a woman (she).
女 is the same character as in 女 (nǚ, woman), so 她 literally contains “woman”.
In speech they are identical. You only know who is meant from the conversation, so in a listening question you must use context.
Memory aid (not etymology): the right part 也 is shared, so cover it with your thumb and look only at the left.

parts.note: Radicals are reused in many characters.

parts.meaning: also (here it mostly hints the sound)

sections.heading: Good to know
sections.body: A third tā, 它, is used for things and animals (“it”). Adding 们 makes it plural: 他们 (tāmen) is a group of men or a mixed group, and 她们 (tāmen) is a group of women.

她.title: 她 (she) vs 他 (he)
她.summary: 她 is tā, “she”. It sounds the same as 他 (he), but the left part is 女, “woman”.

parts.note: Reused in 好 (hǎo, good) and many other characters.

parts.meaning: also (here it mostly hints the sound)

sections.heading: Tips for telling them apart
items: If the left part is 女 you are looking at 她 (she). If it is the thin 亻 it is 他 (he).
Say “woman + also” to yourself when you see 她. It is a memory aid, not the real history.
The two are written differently but spoken identically, so a wrong answer between them is very common. Do not worry, just look left.

好.title: 好 is built from 女 and 子
好.summary: 好 (hǎo, good) is a small picture made from two characters you already know: 女 (woman) and 子 (child).

sections.heading: Built from
sections.intro: Many characters are built from smaller parts that you meet again and again.

sections.heading: Memory aid
items: A woman with her child: something good. This is a story to help you remember, scholars debate the real origin.
You will meet 女 again inside 她 (she), so learning the parts pays off twice.

日.title: 日 (sun / day) vs 月 (moon / month)
日.summary: 日 can mean sun or day; 月 can mean moon or month. Both are common, box-like characters, so compare the inner strokes.

sections.heading: Spot the difference
sections.intro: Compare the insides and the overall shape.

items.note: A squarish, closed box with ONE stroke across the middle.
Narrower and taller, with TWO strokes inside; the left side sweeps outwards at the bottom.

sections.heading: Tips
items: Memory aid, not etymology: imagine 日 as a little sun drawn in a box.
日 is not the same as 口 (kǒu, mouth): 口 is an empty box, 日 has a stroke across the middle.
日 and 月 each have two common meanings (sun / day, moon / month). Context tells you which one is meant.

月.title: 月 (moon / month) vs 日 (sun / day)
月.summary: 月 means moon or month, while 日 means sun or day. Both meanings appear often in beginner Chinese.

items.note: Narrower and taller, TWO strokes inside; the left side sweeps outwards at the bottom.
A squarish, closed box with ONE stroke across the middle.

sections.heading: Two meanings
sections.body: 月 can mean the moon or a month, and 日 can mean the sun or a day. In many phrases the two meanings are not interchangeable translations, so learn them in context.

人.title: 人 (person) and 大 (big)
人.summary: 人 means person. 大 means big. Their shapes are related-looking, but 大 has an extra stroke across the upper body.

items.note: Two strokes, opening out like a person standing.
An extra horizontal stroke crosses the figure.

sections.heading: Memory aid
items: Memory aid, not character history: picture 大 as a person stretching their arms wide to look big.
Count the strokes when the two shapes blur together.

大.title: 大 (big) and 人 (person)
大.summary: 大 means big; 人 means person. The added horizontal stroke is the quickest way to tell 大 apart from 人.

items.note: Has a horizontal stroke across the figure.
Does not have that extra horizontal stroke.

sections.heading: Memory aid
items: Memory aid, not etymology: imagine a person spreading their arms wide to show something is big.

一.title: 一 (one) and its tone changes
一.summary: 一 is yī when said alone, but its tone commonly changes in connected speech. These are pronunciation changes, not different characters.

sections.heading: The common rule
sections.body: 一 is usually yí before a fourth-tone syllable and yì before a first-, second-, or third-tone syllable in common connected-speech patterns. It remains yī when counted or spoken alone.

items.en: one (of something), before a fourth tone

不.title: 不 (bù) changes before a fourth tone
不.summary: 不 means not. It is usually bù alone, but becomes bú before a following fourth-tone syllable in ordinary speech.

sections.heading: The common rule
sections.body: 不 changes from fourth tone bù to second tone bú before a following fourth-tone syllable. The written character stays 不.

items.en: not good (before a third tone, no change)

sections.heading: Remember
items: This is a pronunciation rule in connected speech, not a spelling change.

木.title: 木 (wood / tree) and 目 (eye)
木.summary: 木 and 目 are both pronounced mù, but they mean different things. Look at the shape and the meaning rather than the sound alone.

items.note: Looks like a tree: a cross on top with two legs spreading out below.
A tall narrow box divided by two strokes inside.

sections.heading: Memory aid
items: Memory aid, not etymology: 目 is an eye with lines inside; 木 is a tree with its roots spread out.
Both are read mù, so in a listening question you need the meaning or context, not the sound.

十.title: 十 (ten) and 石 (stone)
十.summary: 十 means ten and 石 means stone. They are pronounced the same in Mandarin (shí), so the sound alone cannot distinguish them.

items.note: Only two crossing strokes.
A long top stroke with a falling stroke, and a 口 box underneath.

sections.heading: How to choose
items: Reading: if there is a 口 box at the bottom, it is 石 (stone). A plain cross is 十 (ten).
Listening: both are shí, so use the sentence to decide which meaning fits.

石.title: 石 (stone) and 十 (ten)
石.summary: 石 means stone and 十 means ten. Both are shí, so they are homophones: the pronunciation is the same.

items.note: A long top stroke with a falling stroke, and a 口 box underneath.
Only two crossing strokes.

sections.heading: Good to know
sections.body: Because 石 and 十 sound the same, listening alone cannot tell you which is meant. The rest of the sentence, or the written character, decides.

女.title: 女 (woman) appears in other characters
女.summary: 女 means woman or female. You have already seen it as the left-hand part of 她 and as one part of 好.

sections.heading: Where you will see 女
sections.intro: A familiar part helps you recognise a new character.

items.note: 女 on the left, 也 on the right.
女 and 子 side by side.

sections.heading: Tips
items: Many characters about women or family use 女 as a part, for example 妈 (mā, mum) and 妹 (mèi, younger sister).
Treat this as a shape-recognition trick, not a claim that a character's meaning is simply the sum of its parts.

子.title: 子 (child) appears in 好
子.summary: 子 means child and is one of the parts in 好 (hǎo, good). The association can help you remember the character.

sections.heading: Where you will see 子
sections.intro: A familiar character can turn up inside a new one.

items.note: 女 and 子 side by side.

sections.heading: Memory aid
items: A woman with a child can be a memory story for 好, but this is not a proven explanation of the character's origin.

上.title: 上 (above) and 下 (below)
上.summary: 上 means above or up; 下 means below or down. Their meanings are opposites and their short strokes sit on opposite sides of a long horizontal line.

items.note: The short stroke sits above the long line.
The short stroke sits below the long line.

sections.heading: Memory aid
items: Use the short stroke as a tiny diagram: above the line for 上, below it for 下.
With 中 (middle) you get the set 上 中 下: above, middle, below.

下.title: 下 (below) and 上 (above)
下.summary: 下 means below or down, the opposite of 上 (above or up). Check where the short stroke sits relative to the long line.

items.note: The short stroke sits below the long line.
The short stroke sits above the long line.

sections.heading: Memory aid
items: This is a visual memory aid: the short stroke shows on which side of the line the meaning lies.
With 中 (middle) you get the set 上 中 下: above, middle, below.

马.title: 马 (horse)
马.summary: 马 means horse. Its shape is distinctive, and it is a useful early character to recognise.

sections.heading: Meaning and sound
sections.body: 马 is pronounced with a third tone. Keep the pitch low in careful isolated pronunciation; in natural speech, the exact contour depends on context.

sections.heading: Memory aid
items: You may imagine the shape as a stylised horse, but treat this as a memory aid rather than a full account of the character's history.

目.title: 目 (eye) and 木 (wood)
目.summary: 目 means eye and is pronounced mù, just like 木 (wood / tree). The extra inner lines help distinguish the written forms.

items.note: A tall narrow box divided by two strokes inside.
A cross with two legs spreading out below.

sections.heading: Memory aid
items: Imagine 目 as an eye with lines inside. This is a memory aid, not a claim about the character's history.
目 is mostly seen inside longer words. In everyday speech people usually say 眼睛 (yǎnjing) for eye.
